1kn21c6:256: The essence of context engineering is solving attention dilution. Transformer attention complexity is O(n²); the longer the context, the more easily key signals are diluted by noise. Context Rot is the most common failure mode. The solution is layered management by usage frequency and stability: the resident layer (identity definition, project conventions, absolute prohibitions) stays short, hard, and executable; the on-demand loading layer (Skills and domain knowledge) keeps descriptors resident and injects full content when triggered; the runtime injection layer (current time, channel ID, user preferences) is assembled per turn as needed; the memory layer (cross-session experience) does not go directly into the system prompt and is read only when needed; the system layer (Hooks or code rules) handles deterministic logic and never enters the context.

1tzyeqq:277: The core problem of multi-Agent collaboration is not parallelism but isolation and collaboration patterns. Two working modes: the conductor mode (a human interacts tightly with a single Agent, adjusting decisions each round, and session-end artifacts disappear) and the coordinator mode (a human appears at the start and end, multiple Agents work in parallel in between, and outputs become persistent artifacts like PRs). Collaboration must first make protocols explicit (message structures structured, stateful, append-only, crash-recoverable), task graph and dependencies defined in advance, and isolation boundaries set up first (sub-Agents have independent messages[] and return only summaries; exploration details stay in the sub-Agent's own context). Under multi-Agent setups, hallucinations amplify each other, so cross-validation is needed to break the error propagation chain.

7slti6:216: Agent evaluation is far more complex than traditional evaluation: you must first prepare tools, runtime environment, and tasks; during execution the Agent calls tools many times to modify environment state; the final score is not based on what it said but on running tests to verify what actually happened in the environment. Common error sources in evaluation systems include: insufficient runtime resources causing processes to be killed, bugs in the grader itself that judge correct answers as failures, test cases disconnected from production scenarios, or looking only at aggregate scores while missing systematic degradation on a certain class of tasks—all of these look exactly like model degradation. The correct order: check the environment first, then touch the Agent.
9wvhcg:236: One of the article's core points: model capability matters, but what determines whether a system runs reliably is often the surrounding engineering conditions. This judgment holds most strongly for highly verifiable tasks like code writing—OpenAI used 3 engineers in 5 months to write a million lines of code and nearly 1,500 PRs, at 10x the speed of traditional development. The reason is not that the model is so powerful, but that the Harness engineering was done right: content the Agent cannot see does not exist (knowledge must live in the codebase itself); constraints are encoded rather than documented (architecture layering is mechanically enforced by custom Linters); end-to-end autonomous task completion (from verification to merge requires no human intervention).

vqe9bi:303: Tool design has gone through three stages: first-generation API wrapping (too fine-grained; the Agent must coordinate multiple tools to achieve a goal) → second-generation ACI (Agent-Computer Interface; tools correspond to Agent goals rather than underlying API operations) → third-generation Advanced Tool Use (Tool Search for dynamic discovery, Programmatic Tool Calling for code orchestration, Tool Use Examples for example-driven usage). The core of ACI principles: tool descriptions state when to use and when not to use; errors are structured with correction suggestions; definitions and implementations are bound together. When debugging an Agent, check tool definitions first, because most tool-selection errors come from inaccurate descriptions, not model capability.
